sections.html: The Discus is regarded by many aquarists as the king of aquarium fish and the most challenging freshwater tropical fish to keep. Adults can reach about 15 cm (6 inches). It was introduced to aquarists in 1933 and made internationally popular by Dr. Herbert R. Axelrod.
Like the Angelfish (Pterophyllum) and Cichlasoma festivum, the Discus inhabits the vast Amazon region, from the middle reaches of the Amazon River far into the flood basins of Venezuela and Peru.

The Discus is commonly found among profuse plant growth in quiet bends of rivers, under overhanging banks and among rock crannies. In shallow areas it cares for its young beneath the leaves of various Nymphaea species.

The absolute minimum aquarium for young Discus is 100 cm long by 50 cm wide and 50 cm tall (40 × 20 × 20 inches). Adult Discus need a 150 cm (5-foot) long aquarium of about 280 litres (75 gallons) minimum to be content and have any chance of breeding successfully. Breeding can happen in a smaller aquarium, but for maximum success a minimum of 280 litres, well planted and well filtered, is suggested. Discus do not like changes in water conditions, and the larger the body of water, the more gradual those changes are.

The Discus needs very pure, clean, clear water, filtered through peat, in a well-established planted aquarium. Temperature should be a steady 28°C (82°F), pH 6.5–7.5, 1–12 dGH.

For breeding: 30°C (86°F), pH 6–6.5, 0–5 dGH.

The Discus is a finicky eater. It is very important to give it a diet of live and frozen food; on a diet of dry flake food it will quickly die, although flakes may be offered occasionally as a supplement.

When rearing fry, the fry feed off the sides of the parents, so both the male and the female need extra protein.

Very peaceful; it does not burrow in the substrate like many cichlids and does not dig up or tear up plants. The Discus lives in harmony with other fish, except at spawning time, when it vigorously defends its young.

It is best to get a group of young Discus and let them pair off; a Discus mates for life. When mates have found each other, they stop staying with the group and stake out their own part of the aquarium as their territory. Only one pair should be left in any one aquarium if successful breeding is wanted. Move the rest of the young to another aquarium, where another pair may find each other.

Can be sexed only by experts. At spawning time the genital papilla is pointed in males and flat and round in females. Viewed from above at breeding time, females are slightly fatter because they are filled with roe (eggs).

For the first 4 days or so the parents move the fry from place to place in the aquarium, much like angelfish. When the fry become free swimming, they go straight to the parent's side. They dig their heads in under a scale and jerk from side to side, breaking off "food" from the parent's skin. Eventually one parent tires of the constant pecking and shakes the fry off, and the fry go to the other parent and do the same. This goes back and forth for weeks, until the young are mature enough to live on their own among the plants.

Seen from the front, Discus are extremely thin for their size, but from the side they are nearly round, hence the name discus, Latin for plate or dish. Their basic body colour in nature is brown. Brilliant blue bars cover both the dorsal and anal fins and extend onto the back and belly. The dorsal, ventral and anal fins are edged in bright red. A variety from Lake Tefé, Brazil, has bright metallic green or blue bars all over the fins and body and is occasionally called the Royal Discus.

Over the decades many varieties have appeared, such as red, yellow and orange, and a yellow-orange burst of colour called the Sunset Discus. These varieties do not come from nature but were developed over many years of careful breeding.
